title: Canucks' 2-9-1 Start Is Backed by the Chances, Not Just the Goaltending
dek: Vancouver sits 32nd in points and 32nd in chance share, and a goalie crisis is only part of what's sinking them.
text:
Twelve games into the season, the Vancouver Canucks are 2-9-1 with 5 points, last in the NHL by points. They have been outscored 56-35. The easy reading is a goaltending collapse on top of some bad bounces. The numbers say something less comfortable: this team has been outplayed in most of its games, and the record is close to what the play deserves.

## How the record was built

Start with chances. Expected goals measures the quality of shots taken, so it tells you how a team played regardless of how the puck went in. The Canucks have generated 28.9 expected goals and allowed 47.2. That is a 38% share of the expected goals, which ranks 32nd in the league. At five-on-five alone the share is 40%, so the problem is not just penalties or one bad special-teams unit. They are giving up far more than they create in ordinary play.

The game-by-game log shows how consistent that is. Vancouver had the better of the chances in just two of 12 games, a 3.61-1.70 expected goals edge over CGY and a 3.61-3.74 near-tie with NYI. Using "deserved to win" (the share of simulated replays of every shot that the team wins), the Canucks cleared 50% once, at 71% against Calgary, a game they won 4-1. Against VGK they deserved to win just 9% of the time (1.51 to 4.49 in expected goals) and lost 2-3. Against DET on Oct. 22 it was 17% (1.91-4.03) and a 2-5 loss. Against CAR on Oct. 20, 15%, and a 3-6 loss.

Not every result was a fair one. The season opened with a 6-5 overtime win at EDM in which Vancouver deserved to win only 22% of the time (2.00 to 3.68 in expected goals). Add the Calgary game and you have both wins. One was earned, one was borrowed.

## Finishing is helping, goaltending is not

Here is the part that complicates the story. Vancouver has scored 6.1 more goals than expected. Shooters have been converting better than their chances predict, which usually fades. If that finishing luck were average, the team would have roughly 29 goals instead of 35 and an even uglier ledger.

The goaltending cuts the other way. Goals saved above expected compares the goals a goalie allowed to what the shots he faced should have produced. As a team the Canucks sit at -8.8. Kevin Lankinen is the main drag: -12.25 goals saved above expected this season, with a .808 save percentage over 8 games (6 starts). Over his last five starts, all losses (0-5-0), he is at .825 and 4.9 goals worse than expected. His last-season figure was -20.31, so this is not a new problem.

Leevi Meriläinen has been better, with a .917 save percentage and +2.35 goals saved above expected in 7 games (6 starts). It is a small sample, but it is a real contrast, and last season he was at -17.93, so we would not bank on it. Still, Vancouver's goalie numbers split in an uncomfortable way: the more-used results are poor, and the better ones are too brief to trust.

Put the two together and the picture is that the goalie is costing the Canucks roughly what the shooters are giving back. Even if goaltending recovered to average, a team with a 38% share of expected goals is not going to climb far.

## Special teams and discipline

The penalty kill is the worst in the league at 32nd, allowing 0.98 expected goals per game. The power play is 27th, generating 0.47 expected goals per game. Neither unit is bailing the team out of tight games. Vancouver takes 3.83 penalties per game and draws 3.58, so they spend slightly more time shorthanded than with the man advantage, and the shorthanded time is the worst part of their game.

## The players

Elias Pettersson leads the team with 12 points (4 goals) in 12 games, playing 19.58 minutes a night. His own expected goals are 2.12 against 4 actual goals, so some of the scoring is finishing above the chances. The team's share of expected goals is 7.55 percentage points better with him on the ice, which is a genuine sign that his play, not just his production, is helping.

Jonathan Lekkerimäki has 4 goals and 9 points in 14.52 minutes, with the team 7.56 points better with him on. Jake DeBrusk leads the club in his own expected goals at 3.76 but has 3 goals on those chances (-0.76), so he is slightly under-finishing. The team is 7.95 points better with him on the ice. Max Sasson is the best driver by that measure at +10.34, with 3 goals and 4 points, and his team has scored 8.6 fewer goals than the chances deserve while he is on the ice. That kind of gap tends to swing back.

At the other end, Paul Cotter has 4 goals on 1.4 expected goals (+2.6), and the team's share is 13.87 points worse with him on the ice. Brock Boeser has 8 points but is -7.35 by the same measure. Brendan Gallagher has 0 goals on 2.17 expected, the biggest shortfall among the regulars, and may be due for a few.

For context from outside the data, Evolving-Hockey's wins above replacement, a one-number estimate of a player's total contribution, from last season (2025-26) rates Linus Karlsson, Filip Hronek and Marco Rossi at 1.6 each, with Pettersson at 0.8. That says the roster has more than this record suggests, at least on paper.

## Will it hold?

Mostly, yes. The nine-game winless run (0-8-1, outscored 41-18) is backed by the chances: Vancouver had 35% of the expected goals in that stretch. The last ten is 1-8-1. A team with this profile, 32nd in chance share, 32nd on the penalty kill and shaky in goal, is not unlucky so much as outmatched in how it plays. The finishing at +6.1 is more likely to cool than the goaltending is to heat up, and that would push things the wrong way.

The upside is narrower. Better goaltending alone is worth several goals, and players like Sasson and Gallagher have scoring to recover. That might turn a few of the one-goal losses (2-3 to VGK, NYI and FLA) into points. It will not fix a team that is conceding quality chances at this rate.

## What to watch

Watch who starts in goal, and whether Meriläinen's numbers hold up over more games. Watch the penalty kill, because 32nd leaves little room to get worse and some room to recover. And watch whether the five-on-five share climbs back toward 45%. If it does, the record has a chance to improve. If it stays near 40%, the standings will keep reflecting what the games have shown.
